title: Synthetic Bio
tagline: Full-stack to harness 4.5 billion years of engineering infrastructure
old_blurb: Biology is the most advanced technology on Earth. Living cells build complex molecules, sense their surroundings, repair themselves, and multiply, all at room temperature and running on little more than sugar. Synthetic biology makes that power programmable: DNA becomes code, and organisms become platforms that can be designed to solve problems nothing else can, from how we make the materials and chemicals industry depends on to how we keep animals healthy.
bullet_points: Programmable Cells: many of the molecules the world depends on are scarce, costly, or impossible to make synthetically. Writing DNA like code lets microbes produce them on demand, along with many that nature never made

Living Factories: most chemicals and materials still start as oil, mined ore, or wild harvest. Fermentation grows them from sugar instead, and because cells copy themselves, a strain proven in a flask can scale to industrial supply
Precision Beyond Chemistry: industrial chemistry runs on heat, pressure, and harsh solvents, and pays for it in energy and waste. Enzymes do the same work in one clean step at room temperature

Healthier Animals: livestock consume much of the world's antibiotics, driving resistance that threatens people too. Vaccines, probiotics, and feed ingredients made by biology protect animals and the food supply without that cost

Resilient Supply: critical ingredients often come from a handful of plants an ocean away, and one disruption empties shelves. Anything that can be brewed can be made close to where it is needed, from local feedstocks

title: National Security
old_blurb: We live in a compromised world, where AI is accelerating every threat vector and the digital landscape leaves us more exploitable than ever before. Threats don't stay in a single lane, so our national security capability pairs cutting-edge technology with tried and true techniques across every domain that matters, at a standard usually reserved for the highest levels of government.
bullet_points: Secure Communications & Infrastructure: power, water, ports, and networks are now front-line targets. They must stay private, trusted, and running while someone is actively trying to break them
Critical Minerals & Supply Chains: rare earths and strategic materials sit inside every chip, battery, and weapon system. Whoever controls their supply sets the pace for everyone else
Signals & Spectrum: every modern operation rides on the electromagnetic spectrum. Owning it means communicating, navigating, and sensing while denying an adversary the same
Next-Gen ISR: seeing first is still the decisive advantage. Low-cost, persistent sensing puts awareness in the hands of the people who need it, without risking lives or scarce assets
Cyber & AI Advantage: AI lets attackers move at machine speed and at scale. Defense has to be faster, and built into systems from the start rather than bolted on
Command & Control Systems: information only matters if it reaches a decision in time. Connecting every sensor, system, and team turns raw data into coordinated action

title: Systems
tagline: AI is only as good as the system it runs on
old_blurb: Most organizations run on ad hoc processes, undocumented knowledge, and data scattered across tools that never talk to each other. Layer AI on top of that and complexity scales faster than capability. Our systems capability makes every role, decision, and workflow defined, visible, and connected, so organizations compound instead of plateau.
bullet_points: People: AI multiplies whatever each person does, good or bad. Clear roles, real accountability, and aligned leadership decide whether that leverage compounds or collides
Processes: AI can only run a process that has been written down. Documented, standardized work is what turns it from a clever demo into a dependable teammate
Technology: AI is only as good as the data it can reach. Connected software and clean, structured data are the difference between real answers and confident guesses
Finances: when execution gets cheap, choosing where to spend becomes the hard part. Clean books and reliable forecasts show which bets are actually paying off
Operations: AI makes everything faster, including mistakes. A steady operating rhythm keeps that speed pointed at the strategy instead of away from it

title: Biomanufacturing
tagline: Even manufacturing that leverages biology as its smallest machines requires innovation with its largest
blurb: Programmable cells are quietly rebuilding the physical economy, replacing extraction and petrochemistry with molecules grown from sugar and air. But scale-up is unforgiving, and the margin between a process that transfers and one that stalls lives in the hardware and the data.
bullet_points: 50 years of stagnation: bioreactors and process equipment are legacy industrial designs, barely changed in decades.
Equipment constrains biology: whole classes of organisms and process regimes are off-limits to today's hardware.
Raised ceiling: limitations in legacy bioreactor designs dramatically limit actualized yields compared to known theoretical limits, leaving headroom to improve output through redesigned hardware.
New hardware unlocks novel processes: altering and adding hardware makes it possible to add highly advantageous steps to the biomanufacturing process.

title: Strain Engineering
tagline: Where every biomanufacturing project must start
blurb: Also known as genetic engineering: DNA programming, host organism editing, and exotic organism harnessing. Most production limitations and failures trace back to the organism itself.
bullet_points: The organism is the biggest bottleneck: most production limitations and failures trace back to the organism itself. Deep expertise in the biomanufacturing process can better inform organism design to optimize for these factors.

Organism optimization should be recursive: doing strain engineering and biomanufacturing prototyping within the same company allows for recursive refinement of the host organism in ways few others can achieve.
Data collection starts at zero: an AI-enabled bio lab needs in-house data on the organisms it engineers and the edited DNA going into them as the first data point in its AI pipelines.

Most organisms are undiscovered or unutilized: the vast majority of microbial organisms in nature have not yet been harnessed for biomanufacturing. Expanding the list of usable organisms dramatically expands possibilities.

title: Molecular Engineering
tagline: The success of any biological product is ultimately determined by its usefulness in the real world
blurb: Programmable cells can now grow therapeutic proteins and peptides, enzymes, crop and animal health actives, sustainable materials, flavors and fragrances, and next-generation food. Each application sets its own bar, and a molecule has to clear it before anything downstream is worth building.
bullet_points: Bench success ≠ field success: molecules optimized for lab benchmarks often underperform in real deployment conditions.
Applications demand tailoring: each use case has its own stability, potency, and formulation requirements.

Target molecule is the first gate: no other part of the biomanufacturing process matters or is worth investing in until customers have de-risked their target molecule and its mechanistic capabilities.

tagline: Bringing commercial biology offerings into the modern era

Buyers are familiar with digital procurement: in most other areas of commerce, buyers can log into a portal, control what they are spending and understand what they are getting. Bio shouldn't be any different.

title: Supply Chain & Logistics
tagline: The systems beneath your systems, mapped, understood, and hardened
blurb: Every operation rests on critical infrastructure and supply chains it does not control, and on people and assets that must move through environments where "usually fine" isn't good enough. Movement is the moment of maximum exposure, yet most itineraries are planned as if it were the safest part of the week.
bullet_points: Downstream fallout: when a supplier is hit, the damage reaches your operations in a specific order and with a specific amount of warning, whether or not you have mapped it.
Compromised inputs: a foreign-directed subcontractor or a substituted component can carry a collection capability into a facility for the life of the structure.
Built before adversaries: operational infrastructure designed in an era that never imagined an adversary now faces one that has several.
Movement is maximum exposure: wrongful detention is a documented state tactic, kidnapping remains an industry, and a region can destabilize between booking and boarding.
Borders read devices: borders now read devices as thoroughly as passports.

title: People
tagline: Every seat defined, every person accountable
blurb: Organizations grow faster than their structure. Roles blur, decisions pile up at the top, and critical knowledge lives in a few people's heads, so when a key employee leaves, the work leaves with them.
bullet_points: Undefined roles: when no one can say exactly what a seat owns, the work falls into the gaps between seats.
Leadership bottlenecks: decisions that belong with the team route back to the founders, throttling the whole organization.
Knowledge walks out the door: undocumented expertise turns every departure into a restart instead of a transition.
Misaligned incentives: compensation that isn't tied to outcomes rewards activity instead of performance.
Hiring without specificity: a loosely scoped role attracts a loosely matched hire, and the cost shows up months later.

title: Processes
tagline: Zero ad hoc, zero undocumented processes
blurb: Most businesses already know what needs to improve. The hard part is the structure, accountability, and follow-through required to make it happen, and processes that live in habits instead of documentation can't be measured, handed off, or automated.
bullet_points: Ad hoc by default: the same task done three ways by three people produces three different outcomes.
Invisible workflows: when work moves through inboxes and hallway conversations, no one can see where it stalls.
No operating cadence: without a consistent rhythm of meetings, metrics, and reviews, priorities drift week to week.
Vague until made precise: the gaps in a process rarely surface until someone tries to write it down.
Nothing to automate: a process that was never defined can't be automated, only accelerated into a bigger mess.

title: Technology
blurb: Technology works best on top of strong systems, clear processes, and structured data. Without that foundation, every new tool adds to the sprawl: another login, another spreadsheet, another source of truth that disagrees with the last one.
bullet_points: Tool sprawl: software bought one problem at a time leaves data spread across systems that never talk to each other.
Unstructured data: AI can't reason about an organization whose information has no consistent definitions or schema.
Implementations that automate confusion: new software dropped onto undefined processes hard-codes the problem instead of fixing it.
No data governance: without clear ownership and access control, sensitive data ends up everywhere and trusted nowhere.
Complexity outpaces capability: without the foundation, each new tool scales complexity faster than results.

title: Finances
blurb: Clean books and reliable reporting are the foundation of sound decision-making, yet many growing businesses run on late closes, loose controls, and forecasts no one trusts. Leadership ends up steering by instinct while the numbers lag behind.
bullet_points: Late, unreliable close: when the books take weeks to close, every decision is made on last quarter's reality.
Weak controls: missing internal controls leave the business exposed to errors, leakage, and an audit it isn't ready for.
Disconnected from operations: financials that don't tie to operational activity can say what happened but never why.
Cash surprises: without forecasting and cash management, growth itself can run a healthy business out of money.
Investor-grade expectations: boards, lenders, and acquirers expect reporting most growing businesses were never built to produce.

title: Operations
tagline: Consistent, efficient, and predictable at every scale
blurb: Many businesses operate with far more potential than their current systems and structure allow. As they scale, the informal ways of working that got them here start to break: teams fall out of sync, capacity runs out without warning, and execution depends on heroics.
bullet_points: Throttled growth: things are going okay, but they could be going much better, and no one has the bandwidth to diagnose why.
Cross-functional friction: hand-offs between teams are where work slows down, gets duplicated, or disappears.
Execution by heroics: outcomes that depend on a few people working harder aren't repeatable, and they don't scale.
Capacity blind spots: without capacity planning, the first sign of a constraint is a missed commitment.
Transactions expose everything: diligence, acquisitions, and integrations surface every operational gap at once, usually at the worst possible time.
